More than a dozen animals from a Martin County hoarding case have found forever homes and the total number of rescued dogs and cats has climbed to 108. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says animals continue to come in from the same case. Sarah Fisher of the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast said every single day more animals are coming forth from the same case.

Fisher said the shelter needs community support to keep up with the growing number of animals in its care. Donations have been pouring in as staff perform spay and neuter surgeries, microchip animals, and clear them medically for adoption every day. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast recommends checking their website for the most up-to-date adoption listings. Those interested in adopting can call or visit the shelter for a meet and greet.

cards.headline: Florida judge considers challenge to Amendment 3 ballot language on property taxes
cards.teaser: A Leon County circuit judge heard arguments Wednesday over whether the ballot title and summary for Amendment 3, a November property-tax measure, fairly explains the proposal or am
cards.body:
A Leon County circuit judge heard arguments Wednesday over whether the ballot title and summary for Amendment 3, a November property-tax measure, fairly explains the proposal or amounts to political advocacy. The amendment would increase the non-school homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 for people who establish permanent Florida residency by Dec. 31, reduce the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead property from 10% to 5%, and require local governments to spend remaining property-tax revenue on public needs such as public safety, schools, infrastructure and natural resources.

Leon County Circuit Judge David Frank heard arguments in three consolidated lawsuits challenging the title and summary scheduled to appear on November ballots. The challengers include the nonprofit Save Our Voters From Misleading Ballot Language, several former mayors, former Republican state Sen. Jeff Brandes and former Democratic U.S. Rep. Al Lawson Jr. They argue the amendment's title, 'Save Our Homes From Excessive Property Taxes,' and phrases promising to benefit taxpayers, protect small businesses, preserve core services and ensure fairness are biased, inaccurate and designed to persuade voters. Plaintiffs' attorney Jamie Cole told the court the language crosses a line and called it the worst example of a biased ballot question he has seen. Frank did not immediately rule, instead ordering attorneys to submit proposed decisions by 5 p.m. Monday.

Attorneys representing the attorney general, secretary of state and Department of State urged Frank to uphold the language. State attorney Ben Gibson argued the title and summary must be read together and that Florida law requires them to explain only the amendment's chief purpose, not every possible consequence or implementation detail. The challengers must prove the title and summary are clearly and conclusively defective, not merely that different wording could have been better, Gibson said. The Legislature approved the proposal during a June special session, passing it 75-26 in the House and 30-9 in the Senate. Because it is a proposed constitutional amendment, it was not subject to the governor's signature or veto. It needs support from at least 60% of voters in November.

A July analysis by Florida's Revenue Estimating Conference projected the quantifiable portions of the amendment would reduce local property-tax collections by nearly $4.93 billion in the 2027-28 fiscal year. The modeled recurring impact is approximately $11.83 billion annually. Election officials told the court that county supervisors may begin printing ballots Aug. 27, adding urgency to the case and any appeal. If Frank finds all of the ballot statements defective and appeals are declined or exhausted, Florida law gives Attorney General James Uthmeier 10 days to submit corrected wording.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue faces $16.5M loss, 116 job cuts if property tax reform passes
cards.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue could lose $16.5 million if voters approve property tax reform in November, according to public records. County commissioners are set to discuss what thos
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli warned Tuesday that a proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could reduce Fire Rescue funding by $9.5 million in the first year and $16.5 million annually by the second year, potentially forcing the closure of three fire stations and the layoff of 116 firefighters. The measure, which will go before Florida voters in November, could lower property tax bills for homeowners but also reduce revenue used to pay for public services. During Tuesday's Martin County Commission meeting, Cianciulli presented a planning exercise outlining how his department could respond to the projected revenue loss.

Under the scenario, Fire Rescue could close Station 18 on Britt Road, Station 33 in Hobe Sound, and Station 23 on Kanner Highway. The $16.5 million annual loss by the second year represents a 22 percent reduction from the department's current budget. The chief said the department could be forced to lay off as many as 116 firefighters by the second year, equivalent to one of the department's three shifts.

Cianciulli warned the funding loss could force Martin County to eliminate specialized teams responsible for hazardous materials incidents, technical rescues and dive operations. The department could then have to request assistance from neighboring agencies in Palm Beach or St. Lucie counties, potentially increasing response times. In an interview after the meeting, Cianciulli pointed to the deadly Camp Mystic flooding in Texas as an example of the delays that can occur when a community must rely on outside resources. He said Martin County already has difficulty recruiting trained firefighter-paramedics because departments farther south offer better compensation.

County leaders have previously said the department has few options to absorb the projected revenue loss because about 93 percent of the Fire Rescue budget is dedicated to personnel. Martin County Commissioner James Blake Capps said higher insurance premiums could result from station closures, as residents living more than five miles from a fire station pay higher homeowner's insurance. Cianciulli advised residents to learn as much as possible about the proposal and its potential effects before casting their ballots in November.

cards.headline: Martin County School District cuts 3 bus routes, saving $255,000
cards.teaser: The Martin County School District has approved a consolidation of bus routes that officials say will save $255,000 without affecting students or eliminating any driver positions.
cards.body:
The Martin County School District has approved a consolidation of bus routes that officials say will save $255,000 without affecting students or eliminating any driver positions. The school board voted Tuesday unanimously to reduce the number of bus routes by 3, bringing the total from 58 to 55 ahead of the upcoming school year. District officials say all bus stops will remain the same and students will not be impacted by the change. Superintendent Michael Maine said the district now has 55 routes and roughly 56 drivers, so all routes are covered.

The $255,000 in savings reflects a reduced transportation budget and will not be redirected to a specific expense, according to the school district. Transportation Director Ruth Spires confirmed that no drivers were let go as part of the consolidation. She said the routes that were consolidated were already being covered by existing drivers due to a shortage last year. Drivers will be paid for any additional hours they work as a result of the consolidation, Spires explained.

Michael Skinner, the President of the local AFSCME labor union chapter, voiced concerns during public comment on behalf of the bus drivers, saying their feedback indicated buses are always full and cutting routes is not a good idea. Spires pushed back on that concern, noting that the buses hold a maximum of 77 passengers and are not operating at capacity. The district said it is confident it will maintain the same level of service with fewer buses on the road.

cards.headline: TCT’s 2026 Summer Reading Picks: 12 Books to Add to Your List
cards.teaser: From brand-new memoirs and literary thrillers to romance, historical fiction and enduring American classics, these 12 books offer a summer reading option for nearly every mood.
cards.body:
Summer reading does not have to mean one particular kind of book. Some days call for a fast-moving crime story or romance that can keep you turning pages by the pool. Others are better suited to a searching memoir, an immersive family saga or a work of nonfiction that leaves you thinking long after you close it.

TCT's 2026 summer reading picks range from newly released books by Colson Whitehead, Tayari Jones, Annie Jacobsen, Patrick Radden Keefe and other major writers to modern favorites and classics worth discovering for the first time. The list includes literary fiction, memoir, romance, true crime, historical fiction and two enduring American novels.

Every synopsis below is intentionally spoiler-free. Use the Quick Picks section to browse the full list, then choose the book that best fits your current reading mood.

All That's Unseen: An Appalachian Memoir by Emilee Hackney

Memoir Pick

In this debut memoir, Emilee Hackney looks back on growing up in the coalfields of southwest Virginia, where family stories, Pentecostal faith and Appalachian identity shaped nearly every part of her world. As the boundaries around her life tighten, an unexpected path to Harvard begins a difficult reexamination of home, belief and her right to trust her own voice.

Memoir readers interested in Appalachia, faith and reclaiming one's voice

A personal story that treats Appalachia with both affection and clear-eyed honesty A strong choice for readers drawn to memoirs about faith, family and self-reinvention

Unsayable: A Life in Writing by Michael Cunningham

For Writers

Michael Cunningham blends memoir with a meditation on the writing life, moving through childhood, first love, early adulthood, marriage and the long process of becoming an author. Rather than offering a conventional how-to manual, he explores why writers keep trying to describe experiences that language can never capture completely.

Writers, devoted readers and anyone curious about how stories take shape

Combines intimate life writing with thoughtful reflections on literary craft Offers inspiration without pretending that creativity follows a simple formula

Cool Machine: A Novel (The Harlem Trilogy) by Colson Whitehead

Crime Fiction Pick

The final volume of Colson Whitehead's Harlem Trilogy follows furniture dealer and reluctant fence Ray Carney and his formidable partner Pepper through three episodes in 1980s New York. A last heist, the downtown art scene and an old family obligation pull them back toward the criminal world as the city around them becomes wealthier, glossier and no less dangerous.

Crime-fiction fans and readers of Whitehead's Harlem Trilogy

A propulsive crime story set against a sharply observed New York in transition The concluding chapter for readers who followed Harlem Shuffle and Crook Manifesto

Country People by Daniel Mason

Literary Escape

Miles Krzelewski is a loving husband and father who is twelve years late finishing a doctorate on Russian folktales. When his wife accepts a position in Vermont, he treats the move as a chance to restart his stalled life. Instead, he falls in with an eccentric cast of neighbors and becomes increasingly fascinated by a strange local legend that may be more than a story.

Readers who like witty literary fiction with folklore and small-town eccentricity

Balances family life, humor, folklore and a gently mysterious premise A summery change-of-scenery novel with an appealingly unusual cast

Kin by Tayari Jones

Book Club Pick

Vernice and Annie grow up as motherless best friends and neighbors in Honeysuckle, Louisiana, but adulthood sends them toward very different worlds. One leaves for Spelman College and a new circle of opportunity; the other follows a restless search for the mother who left her behind. Their stories eventually converge again in a novel about friendship, chosen family and the lasting pull of home.

Book clubs and readers of multigenerational Southern literary fiction

An emotionally rich story of lifelong friendship and diverging paths Built for discussion about family, ambition, belonging and the American South

Biological War: A Scenario by Annie Jacobsen

High-Stakes Nonfiction

Journalist Annie Jacobsen examines how a laboratory accident or deliberate biological attack could develop into a global emergency. Drawing on interviews with experts in government, medicine, science and the military, she traces a possible breakdown across hours, days and weeks, focusing on the systems meant to contain a fast-moving biological threat.

Readers of investigative journalism, public health and national-security nonfiction

Turns a complex national-security subject into an urgent chronological narrative A natural follow-up for readers of Nuclear War: A Scenario

London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe

True Crime Pick

After nineteen-year-old Zac Brettler dies in London, his grieving family begins asking questions that the official explanation does not settle. Their search reveals that Zac had constructed an elaborate second identity and become connected to figures in a dangerous criminal world. Patrick Radden Keefe follows the family through a story of grief, deception and the hidden networks beneath modern London.

Fans of narrative nonfiction, true crime and investigative mysteries

A deeply reported mystery driven by a family's determination to understand what happened Combines intimate human stakes with an investigation into wealth, identity and crime

Great Big Beautiful Life by Emily Henry

Romance Pick

Optimistic writer Alice Scott and Pulitzer-winning journalist Hayden Anderson arrive on a secluded island competing for the same assignment: the chance to write the biography of reclusive heiress Margaret Ives. Margaret gives each writer only pieces of her story and binds them with strict confidentiality, turning their professional rivalry into a literary mystery complicated by an inconvenient attraction.

Romance readers who like writer protagonists and a layered family mystery

Blends romance with a mystery about memory, storytelling and who controls a life story A beach-friendly choice for readers who enjoy sharp banter and slow-building chemistry

My Friends by Fredrik Backman

Friendship Story

Twenty-five years ago, four teenagers found refuge from difficult home lives during long summer days on an abandoned pier. Their friendship eventually inspired a remarkable painting that unexpectedly comes into the care of eighteen-year-old Louisa. Her effort to understand the artwork sends her on a journey toward the seaside town where the friends' story began.

Readers who want a moving, hopeful story about friendship and art

A warm, emotional novel about the ways friendship and art outlive a single moment Moves between youthful connection and a later journey of discovery

The Nightingale by Kristin Hannah

Historical Fiction

In German-occupied France during World War II, sisters Vianne and Isabelle face the same war with very different temperaments. Vianne tries to protect her home and child as danger closes in, while the younger and more defiant Isabelle is drawn toward active resistance. Their parallel stories explore survival, sacrifice and the often-overlooked choices women made during wartime.

Readers seeking sweeping, character-driven historical fiction

An accessible, emotionally intense entry point into World War II historical fiction Centers women's courage, moral choices and the complicated bonds between sisters

East of Eden by John Steinbeck

American Classic

Set in California's Salinas Valley, John Steinbeck's multigenerational novel follows the intertwined Trask and Hamilton families as patterns of rivalry, longing and betrayal echo across decades. Drawing on the biblical story of Cain and Abel, the novel asks whether people are trapped by inheritance and history or remain capable of choosing a different path.

Readers who want an ambitious multigenerational American classic

A sweeping family saga with memorable characters and enduring moral questions A substantial classic for readers ready to settle into a long summer novel

Their Eyes Were Watching God by Zora Neale Hurston

Florida Classic

Zora Neale Hurston's Florida-set classic follows Janie Crawford as she looks back on a life shaped by three marriages, changing ideas of love and a persistent desire to speak in her own voice. Written with lyricism, humor and vivid dialogue, Janie's journey moves through communities and relationships while tracing her growth toward independence and self-knowledge.

Readers of literary classics, Florida history and stories of self-discovery

An essential American novel with a strong Florida connection Combines a deeply personal search for freedom with Hurston's distinctive language and sense of place

A good summer reading list should offer more than one mood. Readers looking for a recent release can start with All That's Unseen, Cool Machine, Country People, Kin, Biological War or Unsayable. Those who want an emotional novel may gravitate toward My Friends, Great Big Beautiful Life or The Nightingale, while East of Eden and Their Eyes Were Watching God provide two very different ways to spend time with an American classic.

Book prices and availability can change, so use the links above to check the current format and price before ordering. Whichever title you choose, the best summer pick is the one that makes you look forward to finding another quiet hour to read.

cards.headline: Neighbor on Silverstream Circle says community worried about child before Fort Pierce infant death
cards.teaser: A neighbor who lived on Silverstream Circle in Fort Pierce for more than a decade said the community worried about how the 3-month-old was being treated but never thought it was that bad.
cards.body:
Tee McMillan, who lived near the Maxwell home on Silverstream Circle in Fort Pierce for more than a decade, said the death of the infant boy is heartbreaking and haunts her. McMillan said when that baby boy died it was just the worst of the worst. She said everyone in the neighborhood worried about how the child was treated but never knew it was that bad.

McMillan said the community never thought that a baby boy would die. She said all anyone wants is justice for the baby. Deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center after the child was brought to the emergency room by the child's grandparents and medical personnel advised responding deputies that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie men flee police at 80 mph, one found hiding on roof of occupied home
cards.teaser: Two men led Port St. Lucie police on a high-speed chase before abandoning their car and fleeing on foot Monday, with one suspect found hiding on the roof of an occupied home.
cards.body:
A suspected drunk driver fled Port St. Lucie police at nearly 80 mph in a 45 mph zone before he and his passenger abandoned their car and ran. According to the Port St. Lucie Police Department, officers attempted to stop a white Acura after observing multiple traffic violations and signs of impaired driving on Southwest Becker Road. Instead of pulling over, the driver accelerated and weaved in and out of traffic, ignoring traffic signs and signals.

 The driver and passenger abandoned the vehicle in a residential driveway near Southwest Idol Avenue before fleeing on foot. A nearby resident called 911 after seeing the two men run from the scene. Police deployed a K-9 and a drone while officers established a perimeter. Both suspects were located, including one who was found hiding on the roof of an occupied home.

 The suspects were identified as Joseph Gary Harris, 42, and Bryan Shawn Baker, 46. Harris was charged with fleeing and eluding law enforcement, burglary of an occupied dwelling, resisting an officer without violence, and loitering or prowling. Baker was charged with resisting an officer without violence and loitering or prowling.

hero.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue faces $16.5M loss, 116 job cuts if property tax reform passes
hero.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue could lose $16.5 million if voters approve property tax reform in November, according to public records. County commissioners are set to discuss what thos
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners heard a presentation Tuesday outlining how a proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could force Martin County Fire Rescue to cut 116 firefighters over the next two years if voters approve the constitutional amendment in November. The cuts would eliminate about one-third of the department's workforce because of reduced property tax revenue tied to the proposed amendment.

Fire Rescue leaders discussed potential operational changes if those revenue reductions occur. Previous county projections have outlined possible station closures, reductions to specialized teams including HAZMAT, Technical Rescue, the dive team and LifeStar, and delays in replacing equipment. County leaders have previously said the department has few options to absorb the projected revenue loss because about 93 percent of the Fire Rescue budget is dedicated to personnel.

Martin County Commissioner James Blake Capps said the cuts could lead to serious consequences for residents. Officials have warned the proposed cuts could lead to longer emergency response times and affect specialized emergency services provided throughout Martin County. Capps said a no-overtime policy for all fire rescue personnel would result in randomized brownouts of stations. He also said higher homeowners insurance premiums would affect residents if stations shut down, since people living within five miles of a fire station receive a break on their insurance.

No vote on firefighter layoffs or fire station closures occurred during Tuesday's meeting. Commissioners received the presentation as they continue evaluating the potential local impacts of the proposed homestead exemption expansion. Voters will have the final say on the constitutional amendment during the November general election.

cards.headline: Martin County moves to rewrite shark fishing rules after complaints about drones, chum
cards.teaser: Martin County commissioners are rewriting beach fishing rules after complaints that shark fishermen are using drones and remote-controlled boats to drop chum offshore and lure sharks closer to swimming areas.
cards.body:
Martin County commissioners are rewriting the rules on fishing from public beaches after complaints that shark fishermen are using drones and remote-controlled boats to drop chum offshore and lure sharks closer to swimming areas. County attorneys told commissioners Tuesday that Florida law allows fishing from public beaches and takes precedence over conflicting county ordinances. Commissioners now plan to repeal or rewrite portions of the county's existing law and replace them with restrictions based on public safety.

 Shark fishing has grown increasingly popular in Martin County, according to residents who addressed commissioners. Some said they are concerned fishermen are putting swimmers at risk by attracting sharks close to shore. Chumming directly from the beach is already prohibited under Florida law, but commissioners heard complaints that some fishermen are using drones or remote-controlled boats to carry bait offshore before dropping it into the water, potentially allowing them to skirt the state restriction.

 County attorneys recommended drafting a new ordinance that complies with state fishing laws while relying on the county's authority to protect public safety and welfare. Under the proposal, fishing could be prohibited from county beaches during lifeguard hours, when swimmers are most likely to be in the water. The revised ordinance would also prohibit fishing from boat docks while boats are being launched or returning to shore. Commissioners directed county staff to draft the new ordinance and bring it back for a future vote.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce residents oppose proposed mega yacht marina at Museum Pointe over concerns for St. Lucie County Regional History Museum
cards.teaser: Residents and history advocates in Fort Pierce are raising concerns over a proposed mega yacht marina at Museum Pointe, fearing the development could displace the area's cultural heritage and the St. Lucie County Regional History Museum.
cards.body:
The Port of Fort Pierce master plan draft for 2026 calls for replacing the existing area at Museum Pointe with large floating docks designed for mega yachts, along with a clubhouse, an event center and a water taxi connecting to Harbour Pointe to the north. The plan also proposes relocating the history museum. Terry Howard, a passionate advocate for St. Lucie County's history, expressed disbelief over the proposed changes.

 This is a gem for the area, and I just can't believe they want to put mega yachts here, he said. The museum, it's our culture. It's the center for our culture for this county.

 In a statement, St. Lucie County said that no plans have been approved and feedback from the board will dictate future changes, modifications and clarifications to the draft document. Howard has started a petition opposing the proposed marina, hoping to raise awareness and preserve the location and its natural surroundings. This is just a really fantastic place, and our history is capsulized in this museum here, he said. The draft of the master plan is expected to go before the county commission in August.

cards.headline: Martin County School District consolidates bus routes to save $255,000
cards.teaser: The Martin County School District approved changes to its bus routes for the upcoming school year, aiming to improve efficiency and reduce costs.
cards.body:
The Martin County School District approved changes to its bus routes for the upcoming school year, aiming to improve efficiency and reduce costs. The new routes, which will begin on August 10, will consolidate existing routes while keeping bus stops and buses unchanged from last year. The district said the changes will save $255,000.

 The changes address a decline in ridership and will save the district the cost of operating three bus routes, according to Ruth, the district's director of transportation. The district also cited a shortage of bus drivers as part of the reason for the decision. No jobs were lost as a result of the changes.

 Parents can track their child's bus route in real time using the MyReaxium app. The route changes also include activity buses for after-school programs.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County commissioners deadlock on infrastructure tax renewal, postpone decision
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County commissioners split evenly on when to schedule a referendum to renew the county's half-cent infrastructure sales tax, voting unanimously to postpone the decision u
cards.body:
St. Lucie County commissioners split evenly on when to schedule a referendum to renew the county's half-cent infrastructure sales tax, voting unanimously to postpone the decision until August 4. The voter-approved tax expires in December 2028 after its 10-year authorization. Commissioners must decide whether to ask voters to extend it in 2026 or wait until 2028. If they wait and voters approve it then, it would be considered a new tax rather than a continuation.

 Before the commission's discussion on July 21, three Port St. Lucie officials urged the board to place the referendum on the 2026 ballot. Port St. Lucie Public Works Director Colt Schwerdt said the tax has funded road, sidewalk, stormwater and water-quality improvements that have benefited city residents. Utility Systems Director Kevin Matyjaszek said there is a direct correlation between infrastructure and quality of life. Communications Director Sarah Prohaska read a letter from Kenneth Kroll, chairman of both the county and Port St. Lucie Sales Tax Oversight committees, who urged commissioners to act this year.

 Commissioner James Clasby opposed placing the measure on the 2026 ballot, saying he did not want it on the same ballot as Amendment 3 and the School Board tax. Commissioner Erin Lowry agreed, saying many residents are struggling financially and may reject the measure simply because it includes the word tax. Chairwoman Jamie Fowler argued the county would have two opportunities if the measure were placed on the 2026 ballot. Commissioner Cathy Townsend agreed and moved to keep the referendum on the 2026 ballot, but the motion failed on a 2-2 vote.

 With Vice Chairman Larry Leet absent and the commission deadlocked, members voted 4-0 to continue the item until August 4, when Leet is expected to return and cast the deciding vote. Deputy County Administrator Mayte Santamaria reminded commissioners they had already approved an ordinance in March scheduling the referendum for November 2026. Keeping that date requires no action, while delaying it until 2028 would require rescinding the ordinance and adopting a new one.

cards.headline: Indiantown Village Council rejects second attempt at data center pause
cards.teaser: Two Indiantown Village Council members failed to convince colleagues to approve a pause on data center applications, with the village attorney warning the move would violate state legislation.
cards.body:
Indiantown Village Councilwoman Karen Onsager moved that the Village of Indiantown establish a 90-day administrative pause on the acceptance, processing and approval of all new applications for large-load data center development projects during the July 13 budget workshop. The motion died after no council member offered a second. Onsager had requested the pause to allow the council and residents to better understand current and projected demands on water and electrical infrastructure through an informational meeting with technical experts, representatives from the South Florida Water Management District and utility providers.

 Village Attorney Wade Vose said such an administrative pause, whether 90 days or 12 months, would violate Senate Bill 180. Vose said he received an email that same afternoon from a local land use attorney who represents multiple developers within the Village, warning that SB 180 would prohibit anything along the lines of a regulation that would inhibit the process of applications for development. Mayor Carmine Dipaolo warned colleagues about offending state officials who have given the village over $120 million in funding.

 The council previously sought advice from Vose last month on a moratorium after scores of local residents protested the village's preliminary review of a data center application submitted by Nelson Ferreira, which he withdrew on April 29. Village Manager Taryn Kryzda confirmed the industrially zoned lands within the village allowed data centers as a permitted use. Onsager confirmed with Kryzda that a community meeting would be scheduled for Saturday, Aug. 2.

cards.headline: 2 men force victim to withdraw cash at Wells Fargo ATM in Fort Pierce armed robbery
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police are searching for two men in their early 20s who forced a victim to withdraw cash at gunpoint from a Wells Fargo ATM on Sunday night.
cards.body:
A man using a Wells Fargo ATM in Fort Pierce became the victim of an armed robbery on Sunday at about 8:38 p.m. when two men forced him to pull out cash before fleeing on foot. The Fort Pierce Police Department said one of the men displayed a gun concealed in his waistband before forcing the victim to withdraw an unknown amount of cash. Officers responded to the scene, established a perimeter, and used a K-9 and drone to search for the suspects, but the suspects were not located.

 Police described the suspects as two men in their early 20s, about 5 feet 10 inches tall and weighing about 170 pounds. The armed suspect was last seen wearing jeans and a gray hooded sweatshirt. The Fort Pierce Police Department is asking anyone with information to contact the department.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce police seek help identifying suspects in Recreation Center vandalism and vehicle burglaries
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police are asking for the public's help identifying people shown in surveillance images connected to two separate investigations involving vandalism at the Fort Pierce Recreation Center and vehicle burglaries in the Lawnwood Circle area.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police are asking for the public's help identifying people shown in surveillance images connected to two separate investigations involving vandalism and vehicle burglaries. Police said the vandalism occurred at about 4 p.m. July 24 at the Fort Pierce Recreation Center, located at 903 S.

 An unidentified woman was captured on camera damaging city property. Police said multiple air-conditioning units, a trailer and a storage shed were damaged.

 The second investigation involves a series of vehicle burglaries reported during the overnight hours of July 27 in the Lawnwood Circle area. Police said the burglaries occurred in the 1300 block of Nebraska Avenue and the 1300 block of Peppertree Trail, primarily between 2 a.m. and 4 a.m. Investigators said several vehicles were burglarized.

 Some had been left unlocked, while others had windows smashed to gain entry. Surveillance footage showed several people in the area wearing hoodies, shorts and backpacks.

 The department stressed that the vandalism and vehicle burglary cases are separate investigations. Anyone who recognizes the people pictured or has information about either case is asked to contact Fort Pierce police at 772-467-6800 or 772-462-6800. Anonymous tips can be submitted to Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at tcwatch.org. Police also reminded residents to lock their vehicles, remove valuables from plain view and report suspicious activity immediately.

cards.headline: St. Lucie detective calls Fort Pierce baby death case one of worst in 20-year career
cards.teaser: Detective Jennifer Diaz described the Fort Pierce mobile home where a 3-month-old infant died as extremely hot with a bug infestation and unsafe for walking.
cards.body:
Detective Jennifer Diaz of the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office called the death of a 3-month-old infant in Fort Pierce one of the worst cases she has worked in her 20-year law enforcement career. The mobile home in the 800 block of Silverstream Circle was in pretty bad condition, extremely hot, with a bug infestation and a lack of food, Diaz said during a press briefing on July 27. Court documents describe the infant's ribs as more prominent than its stomach.

 The investigation began on August 20, 2025, when deputies went to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center after the 3-month-old child was brought to the emergency room and pronounced dead on arrival. The ultimate causes of death determined by the medical examiner were malnutrition and dehydration. Diaz said the investigation took nearly a year because it was very complicated and required seeking outside experts. The child's mother, Nicole Maxwell, 27, the child's grandfather, Robert Maxwell, 61, and his girlfriend, Vikki Koon, 38, were arrested and charged with aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse.

cards.headline: Stuart man arrested after leading police on chase, crashing into vehicle
cards.teaser: David Kingsley Jr., 31, faces multiple charges after fleeing a traffic stop Tuesday night and leading officers on a pursuit through Stuart and Martin County.
cards.body:
A Stuart man is facing multiple charges after police said he led officers on a chase through Stuart and Martin County Tuesday night. An officer with the Stuart Police Department attempted to stop a vehicle on July 28 for an equipment violation after learning the registered owner's driver's license had been revoked.

 The driver did not stop and instead sped away, leading officers on a brief pursuit through the city. During the chase, the suspect crashed into another vehicle and continued driving out of Stuart. The driver continued driving recklessly into Martin County, where deputies with the Martin County Sheriff's Office and troopers with the Florida Highway Patrol joined the pursuit.

 The vehicle was eventually stopped, and the driver surrendered without further incident. The driver was identified as 31-year-old David Kingsley Jr. He was arrested and charged by Stuart Police with fleeing and eluding law enforcement and leaving the scene of a crash involving property damage. Additional charges were filed by the Florida Highway Patrol and the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

cards.headline: New supplemental radar installed in Fort Myers expected to improve tornado and storm detection for Treasure Coast
cards.teaser: A new supplemental radar at the Fort Myers Public Safety Center is expected to be operational within days and will give forecasters a better view of storms moving toward the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County.
cards.body:
A new supplemental radar at the Fort Myers Public Safety Center is expected to be operational within days. The installation is the first of four new radars planned for Florida by Climavision, the weather technology company working to close low-level radar coverage gaps across the state. Tara Goode, vice president of radar operations at Climavision, said the radar will give forecasters a better view of storms moving toward the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County.

 One of Florida's largest gaps in low-level radar stretches from Lee County through Palm Beach and southern Martin counties. Low-level radar, near 3,000 feet, is the most critical tier for spotting flash flooding and tornadoes. Former National Weather Service meteorologist Brian Lamarre warned that new research shows tornadoes are forming closer to the ground, making low-level radar more important than ever.

 One of the four new Climavision radars planned for Florida will be installed in Palm Beach County, potentially within the next year. Jason Hallstrom, executive director of Florida Atlantic University's Sensing Institute, said supplemental radar alone is not a complete solution and that Florida needs many more than just four of these weather radars across the area.

hero.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue faces $16.5M loss, 116 job cuts if property tax reform passes
hero.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue could lose $16.5 million if voters approve property tax reform in November, according to public records. County commissioners are set to discuss what thos
hero.body:
Martin County Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli warned commissioners Tuesday that proposed property tax reform on the November ballot could force the department to cut as many as 116 firefighters over the next two years and close firehouses across the county. The reform would expand homestead exemptions, potentially reducing the department's budget and forcing major reductions in service.

Among the potential cuts outlined by Cianciulli are closing firehouses, ending hazmat, dive, and technical rescue programs, grounding the department's critical care helicopter, and using firefighting tools past their operational lifetime. The chief said the department would have to call outside agencies when incidents exceed the capabilities of remaining crews and equipment.

Residents who attended the commission meeting expressed mixed reactions. One resident called fire service valuable, while another questioned why cutting personnel pay was not considered as an option. Commissioners also expressed differing views, with Commissioner Edward Ciampi suggesting belt tightening and slashing budgets elsewhere, while Commissioner Eileen Vargas said the county only has so many dollars to go around.

No decisions were made Tuesday. The presentation was an opportunity to gather information so the county can plan accordingly ahead of the November vote.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce residents fight plan to replace Museum Pointe Park with mega-yacht marina
cards.teaser: A proposal to transform Museum Pointe, a public waterfront park in Fort Pierce along the Indian River Lagoon, into a mega-yacht marina has drawn nearly 800 petition signatures from
cards.body:
A proposal to transform Museum Pointe, a public waterfront park in Fort Pierce along the Indian River Lagoon, into a mega-yacht marina has drawn nearly 800 petition signatures from opponents. The Port of Fort Pierce's updated 2026 Master Plan calls for redeveloping the park, which currently features a history center, public waterfront access, fishing piers, and green space, into a facility with floating docks, a multi-story marina, an event center, a waterfront restaurant, and a clubhouse.

 Terry Howard, a volunteer at the History Center at Museum Pointe Park, said development threatens one of the city's most treasured public spaces. The museum has preserved artifacts from Florida's Native American tribes, Spanish shipwrecks, and more for over 50 years. The master plan's renderings place the proposed marina clubhouse exactly where the museum stands today.

 Howard said the concern extends beyond the museum's fate to the loss of public waterfront access. St. Lucie County spokesperson Erick Gill said the museum's future is not in jeopardy if the project moves forward, and that staff has been discussing better locations for the history center for years because it sits on a barrier island in a flood zone.

 Gill said the museum and its collection would be preserved and relocated if the project proceeds. He added that the master plan is designed to expand economic development, create jobs, and generate county revenue. Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the city will have the final say on whether the project moves forward, and that commissioners will have to weigh economic benefits against preserving waterfront access. Broderick said the city must be careful not to eliminate public access to the waterway.

 St. Lucie County leaders are scheduled to discuss the proposal and its current status at a 9 a.m. meeting at the St. Lucie County Commission Chambers. Howard said the stakes go beyond the present. The museum has been at Museum Pointe since the 1970s, and once the area is developed, the public waterfront space will never be replaced.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie bans gas station on Tradition commercial site after months of resident concerns
cards.teaser: The Port St. Lucie City Council has permanently banned construction of a gas station on a 9.4-acre commercial parcel at the southwest corner of Crosstown Parkway and Fairgreen Driv
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council has permanently banned construction of a gas station on a 9.4-acre commercial parcel at the southwest corner of Crosstown Parkway and Fairgreen Drive in Tradition. The council unanimously approved the restriction on July 13 as part of the 16th amendment to the Tradition Master Planned Unit Development, ending nearly three months of debate over the future of land originally planned as Phase 3 of the Heritage Oaks at Tradition residential development.

 Winding River Crosstown LLC requested permission in May to convert the parcel from residential to commercial use. While council members supported commercial development, several raised concerns that a convenience store with gas pumps would worsen traffic along Crosstown Parkway west of Interstate 95. Vice Mayor Jolien Caraballo and other council members asked staff to determine whether gas stations could be eliminated as a permitted use, leading the council to table the request on May 26. Heritage Oaks residents urged the council in June to reject the land-use change, citing traffic, noise and neighborhood impacts.

 The council voted 4-0 on June 22 to approve the commercial designation after the developer agreed to permanently give up the right to build a gas station. The July 13 ordinance codified that restriction into the Tradition MPUD documents, ensuring the prohibition remains with the property regardless of future ownership. City planner Bridget Kean said service stations remain permitted elsewhere in the Tradition mixed-use area but are now prohibited on Parcel 11A. The updated plan also requires the developer to install a fence along the southern property line before mass grading and to complete an architectural wall and landscape buffering along the southeastern and southern boundaries before the first building permit is issued.

 Councilman Anthony Bonna defended the public process and the decision, saying Port St. Lucie has long lacked commercial development, placing a burden on homeowners. Councilman David Pickett said the city has consistently heard residents oppose additional housing and called the shift to commercial the best outcome for the corner. Councilwoman Stephanie Morgan, who initially questioned whether prohibiting a specific business type amounted to government interference, ultimately voted with the council. Mayor Shannon Martin confirmed the restriction would remain with the property in perpetuity before the final unanimous vote.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce residents oppose proposed mega yacht marina at Museum Pointe over concerns for St. Lucie County Regional History Museum
cards.teaser: Residents and history advocates in Fort Pierce are raising concerns over a proposed mega yacht marina at Museum Pointe, fearing the development could displace the area's cultural heritage and the St. Lucie County Regional History Museum.
cards.body:
The Port of Fort Pierce master plan draft for 2026 calls for replacing the existing area at Museum Pointe with large floating docks designed for mega yachts, along with a clubhouse, an event center and a water taxi connecting to Harbour Pointe to the north. The plan also proposes relocating the history museum. Terry Howard, a passionate advocate for St. Lucie County's history, expressed disbelief over the proposed changes.

 This is a gem for the area, and I just can't believe they want to put mega yachts here, he said. The museum, it's our culture. It's the center for our culture for this county.

 In a statement, St. Lucie County said that no plans have been approved and feedback from the board will dictate future changes, modifications and clarifications to the draft document. Howard has started a petition opposing the proposed marina, hoping to raise awareness and preserve the location and its natural surroundings. This is just a really fantastic place, and our history is capsulized in this museum here, he said. The draft of the master plan is expected to go before the county commission in August.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce pizza shop transforms patio into free reading room for children
cards.teaser: Big Apple Pizza in Fort Pierce is converting its outdoor patio into a dedicated reading room where children can pick up free books any time they visit. Owner Scott Van Duzer has op
cards.body:
Big Apple Pizza in Fort Pierce is converting its outdoor patio into a dedicated reading room where children can pick up free books any time they visit. Owner Scott Van Duzer has operated a free book program inside the restaurant for years, but the collection has grown too large for the indoor space.

 Van Duzer said the patio transformation addresses the space shortage while making books more accessible to young readers. Children can take home any book they want at no charge, whether their family stops in for pizza or just to browse the collection. The program aims to encourage a lifelong love of reading and remove barriers to book access.

 Van Duzer said his commitment to giving back stems from lessons he learned from his mother while growing up. He said she taught him that if he could give back, he should give back, and the restaurant lives that principle every day. Watching children get excited about discovering new books has been one of the most rewarding parts of the program.

 Construction on the reading room is underway and is expected to be completed later this fall. Until then, children can continue picking up free books inside Big Apple Pizza at 2311 S 35th St in Fort Pierce, where every child remains welcome to take a book home.

cards.headline: Treasure Coast single-family home prices rise after two-year decline
cards.teaser: Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after drops from 2023 to 2025. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St.
cards.body:
Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after drops from 2023 to 2025. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000. Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000.

 Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that the prices are going to come back down. Inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers.

 Cara Collins, who bought her Martin County home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell. Collins said current prices are higher than she would hope for, and that the market has changed what would be possible for her family today. She said she would not be able to be a stay-at-home mom and be able to afford a home for her kids if buying now.

 Condos and townhomes show different trends. Prices have dropped in Martin and St. Lucie counties and only increased by less than a percent in Indian River County. Decowski said buyers need to come in pre-approved before they go looking at homes, and sellers need to price their homes realistically and present a well-maintained product.

hero.headline: Blue Jays outlast St. Lucie Mets 14-9 in Dunedin slugfest
hero.teaser: Yovanny Rodriguez and Bohan Adderley hit their first St. Lucie home runs, but Dunedin scored six unanswered runs after the Mets briefly took a 9-8 lead.
hero.body:
The St. Lucie Mets hit three home runs and briefly rallied into the lead Wednesday night, but the Dunedin Blue Jays scored six unanswered runs over the final three innings to win 14-9 at TD Ballpark.

 The loss evened the series at one game apiece. St. Lucie has scored 51 runs over its last five games but has allowed 52, going 2-3 during that stretch.

 Yovanny Rodriguez gave the Mets a 3-0 lead in the first inning with a three-run homer, his first since joining St. Lucie from the Florida Complex League.

 Dunedin answered quickly. JoJo Parker hit a two-run homer off Owen Woodward in the bottom of the first, then connected for another two-run shot against Jose Lopez in the second. Parker, the Blue Jays’ top prospect, finished 3-for-4 with two home runs, a single, a walk, four RBIs and four runs scored.

 St. Lucie trailed 8-6 entering the fifth before Simon Juan and Bohan Adderley hit back-to-back home runs with two outs. Juan’s two-run shot tied the game, and Adderley followed with his first St. Lucie homer to put the Mets ahead 9-8.

 The lead held until the seventh, when Dunedin scored four runs against reliever Zack Mack. Parker opened the rally with a hard infield single that first baseman Branny De Oleo stopped, but De Oleo’s throw toward second base escaped into the outfield and allowed Jake Cook to score the tying run.

 Juan Sanchez then chopped a two-run single to give the Blue Jays an 11-9 lead and later scored on a wild pitch. Dunedin added two more runs in the eighth on RBI singles by Brayden Martin and Blaine Bullard.

 After Adderley’s go-ahead homer, Dunedin relievers Noah Palmese, Ricky Tiedemann, Isaac Williams and Dax Dathe combined to retire 10 consecutive Mets batters.

 Elian Peña ended that streak with a leadoff single in the ninth and reached third on an error with no outs. The Mets had a chance to score in double figures for a fourth consecutive game, but Bradley Wilson struck out three straight batters to strand Peña at third.

 Peña went 2-for-4 with two singles and two RBIs, while Adderley finished 2-for-4. Eight of St. Lucie’s nine starters recorded at least one hit.

 Dylan Carey, an undrafted free agent from Nebraska, made his professional debut and went 1-for-3 with a single, a hit-by-pitch and a run scored. He also played error-free defense at shortstop.

 Elwis Mijares provided the strongest outing from the Mets bullpen, pitching 2⅓ scoreless innings with three strikeouts. Woodward, pitching on a minor league rehabilitation assignment, worked the first inning and ended his appearance with consecutive strikeouts.

 Lopez followed Woodward and allowed six runs on four hits and six walks over 2⅔ innings. Mack took the loss after being charged with four runs in two-thirds of an inning.

 Sanchez finished 2-for-4 with a double, two walks and four RBIs for Dunedin. Cook reached base in each of his final five plate appearances with three singles and two walks.

 The Mets fell to 12-19 in the second half and 45-52 overall. The Blue Jays improved to 14-17 in the second half and 45-51 overall.

 The teams play the third game of the series Thursday at TD Ballpark. First pitch is scheduled for 6:30 p.m.

cards.headline: Draft picks power new-look St. Lucie Mets in 14-6 rout of Dunedin
cards.teaser: Four 2026 draft picks combined for nine hits and three home runs, while Clay Holmes threw four scoreless innings in a rehab appearance.
cards.body:
Four members of the New York Mets’ 2026 draft class made immediate impacts Tuesday night as the St. Lucie Mets overwhelmed the Dunedin Blue Jays 14-6 at TD Ballpark.

 Aiden Robbins, Ryan Tayman, John Smith III and Kooper Schulte combined to go 9-for-17 with three home runs, two doubles, seven RBIs and seven runs scored in their professional debuts. The St. Lucie lineup also featured Yovanny Rodriguez and Wyatt Vincent, who made their team debuts after being promoted from the Florida Complex League.

 The revamped offense provided more than enough support for New York Mets pitcher Clay Holmes, who moved his rehabilitation assignment from Triple-A Syracuse to the Florida State League because of predicted bad weather in New York.

 Holmes, recovering from a right fibula injury, scattered two singles and two walks over four scoreless innings. He struck out three and threw 59 pitches.

 Tayman gave St. Lucie a 2-0 lead in the second inning by hitting a two-run home run on the first swing of his professional career. The ninth-round selection out of Cal Poly finished 4-for-5 with a homer, a double, two singles, three runs scored and two RBIs.

 Robbins, a third-round pick from Texas, drove an RBI double off the center-field wall in the third inning for his first professional hit.

 The Mets added three runs in the fourth. Cole Mathis delivered a sacrifice fly before Marco Vargas lined a two-run double off the left-field wall against Dunedin starter Blake Purnell, extending the lead to 6-0.

 Smith, a 19th-round pick from UCF, hit a two-run homer off Purnell in the fifth inning for his first professional hit. He homered again in the ninth and finished 2-for-5 with three RBIs.

 Austin Warren, beginning a rehabilitation assignment for a right forearm strain, pitched a scoreless fifth inning with one strikeout and induced a double play. He was credited with the win.

 Dunedin scored four runs against Tyler McLoughlin in the sixth, but Ernesto Mercedes stopped the rally with consecutive strikeouts. Mercedes then retired the Blue Jays in order in the seventh and added two more strikeouts.

 Elian Peña hit a two-run homer in the eighth, and Robbins added an RBI single to push St. Lucie’s lead to 11-4.

 The Mets scored three more runs in the ninth on Smith’s second homer, a bases-loaded walk by Julio Zayas and an RBI single from Vargas. Vargas finished 3-for-5 with three RBIs.

 Schulte, a 20th-round pick from Iowa, went 1-for-3 with a single, a walk, a hit-by-pitch and two runs scored. Rodriguez went 1-for-4 with a walk and two runs in his St. Lucie debut, while Vincent went 1-for-4 with a double, a walk and a run.

 The Mets improved to 12-18 in the second half and 45-51 overall. Dunedin fell to 14-16 in the second half and 44-51 overall.

 The teams continue the series Wednesday at TD Ballpark. First pitch is scheduled for 6:30 p.m.

cards.headline: St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware named FSL Pitcher of the Week
cards.teaser: The 22-year-old left-hander struck out 12 batters over seven scoreless innings in two appearances against Fort Myers.
cards.body:
St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware has been named the Florida State League Pitcher of the Week for July 20-26, Minor League Baseball announced Monday.

 Ware made two appearances against the Fort Myers Mighty Mussels at Clover Park, starting Tuesday and returning for a relief outing Sunday. The left-hander combined to throw seven scoreless innings, allowing three hits and two walks while striking out 12 batters.

 The Mets won both games in which Ware appeared. He earned the victory Sunday after pitching four scoreless innings, allowing one hit and one walk and recording a career-high eight strikeouts as St. Lucie rallied for an 11-8 win.

 Ware, 22, was selected by the New York Mets in the 15th round of the 2025 MLB Draft out of LSU. He made his professional debut with St. Lucie in April and has remained with the team throughout the season.

cards.headline: Mets erase 5-0 deficit to beat Mighty Mussels 11-8
cards.teaser: Jeremy Rodriguez went 4-for-4, and Conner Ware struck out a career-high eight as St. Lucie scored eight runs in the second inning.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie Mets erased an early five-run deficit with an eight-run second inning and rallied for an 11-8 win over the Fort Myers Mighty Mussels on Sunday afternoon at Clover Park.

 Fort Myers won the seven-game series 4-3 and finished the season series with an 8-4 advantage.

 The Mighty Mussels scored three runs in the first inning and two more in the second to build a 5-0 lead. St. Lucie responded with eight runs in the bottom of the second and moved ahead for good.

 Randy Guzman delivered the decisive hit, lining a two-out, two-run single that turned a 5-4 deficit into a 6-5 Mets lead. Julio Zayas followed with a two-run single to extend the advantage to 8-5.

 The Mets added three runs in the third. Elian Peña hit an RBI single, Jacob Reimer drove in a run with a double and Trey Snyder added a sacrifice fly to make it 11-5.

 Conner Ware took over on the mound in the third inning and settled the game down for St. Lucie. Ware pitched four scoreless innings, allowed one hit and one walk, and struck out a career-high eight batters. He struck out the side swinging in the fourth and struck out the side looking in the sixth before earning the win.

 Fort Myers scored three runs in the seventh against Luis Sotillo, who was making his Mets debut. Sotillo recovered by retiring six of the final seven batters he faced and carried the game through the eighth inning.

 Elwis Mijares worked a perfect ninth on six pitches to record his third save.

 Jeremy Rodriguez led the Mets at the plate, going 4-for-4 with a double, an RBI and two runs scored from the No. 9 spot in the order. Zayas and Peña collected two hits apiece.

 Reimer, beginning a minor league rehabilitation assignment for a groin injury, went 1-for-3 with a double, a walk, two RBIs and two runs scored. He played all nine innings at third base.

 The Mets improved to 11-18 in the second half and 44-51 overall. They are off Monday before opening a six-game road series against the Dunedin Blue Jays on Tuesday. First pitch at TD Ballpark is scheduled for 6:30 p.m.

cards.headline: St. Lucie Mets Fall Short in 15-14 Loss to Fort Myers
cards.teaser: Randy Guzman hit two home runs and drove in six as the St. Lucie Mets nearly erased an eight-run deficit in a 15-14 loss to Fort Myers.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie Mets nearly erased an eight-run first-inning deficit but fell one run short in a 15-14 loss to the Fort Myers Mighty Mussels on Saturday night at Clover Park.

 Fort Myers scored eight runs in the opening inning and survived several St. Lucie rallies to earn its third consecutive victory.

 Mets starter Ethan Lanthier was charged with seven runs on five hits and two walks before being removed with two outs in the first inning. Harry Genth delivered a three-run double during the Mussels' early outburst.

 Mets Answer With Five-Run First Inning

 St. Lucie immediately responded with five runs against Fort Myers starter Matt Barr in the bottom of the first. Antonio Jimenez, Branny De Oleo and Simon Juan each recorded RBI hits to cut the deficit to 8-5.

 The Mighty Mussels added three runs against Franyel Diaz in the third inning. Ramiro Dominguez drove in two with a single, and Byron Chourio hit a solo home run to extend the Fort Myers lead to 11-5.

 Trey Snyder helped St. Lucie pull closer in the fourth inning with an unconventional trip around the bases. Snyder's ground-ball single was mishandled by shortstop Quetin Young, who then committed a throwing error that allowed Snyder to score and another run to cross the plate.

 The play cut the Mussels' lead to 11-7.

 Guzman Homers Twice

 Randy Guzman hit a two-run homer against Ramiro Villanueva in the fifth inning to bring the Mets within two runs.

 Villanueva later hit consecutive batters and was ejected. St. Lucie loaded the bases with one out, but reliever Adam Falinski retired Elian Pena on a popout and Snyder on a groundout to preserve the 11-9 Fort Myers advantage.

 Young answered with a three-run home run over the batter's eye in the sixth, pushing the Mussels' lead to 14-9.

 Guzman responded again in the bottom half of the inning, launching a three-run homer to make it 14-12.

 He finished the game 3-for-4 with two home runs, a single, six RBIs and two runs scored.

 Ninth-Inning Rally Falls One Run Short

 Ricardo Paez opened the ninth inning with a solo home run that gave Fort Myers a 15-13 lead and provided what proved to be a crucial insurance run.

 Francisco Toledo scored on a wild pitch and throwing error with one out in the bottom of the ninth. Marco Vargas then homered to right field with two outs, pulling St. Lucie within one run at 15-14.

 Brent Francisco struck out Chase Meggers to end the game and record his third save.

 Michael Hilker Jr. earned the win after pitching 2 1/3 scoreless innings of relief for Fort Myers. Lanthier took the loss.

 Jimenez went 2-for-3 with two walks and three runs scored. Vargas, De Oleo and Juan added two hits apiece.

 The Mets fell to 10-18 in the second half and 43-51 overall. The Mighty Mussels improved to 14-14 in the second half and 51-42 overall.

 The teams will conclude their series Sunday at Clover Park. First pitch is scheduled for 12:10 p.m.

cards.headline: Messi bathed Yamal as baby in 2007 photo shoot, now they meet in World Cup final
cards.teaser: A 2007 charity calendar photo shoot paired teenage Lionel Messi with infant Lamine Yamal. Now 19 years later, they face off in Sunday's World Cup final.
cards.body:
Photographer Joan Monfort took photos in 2007 of a teenage Lionel Messi bathing infant Lamine Yamal in a plastic bathtub as part of a charity calendar produced by local newspaper Sport and UNICEF. Monfort, who works as a freelance photojournalist for The Associated Press, took the photos after Yamal's mother won a raffle of families in the city of Mataró near Barcelona who wanted to participate.

 Soccer destiny paired her baby boy with the Argentine who would become the greatest of all time. Messi left Barcelona in 2021 when the club was in financial trouble. Yamal erupted at the club two years later.

 Monfort had no recollection of the photos until Yamal's father posted one on social media during the 2024 European Championship, when a teenage Yamal led Spain to the title. The photo went viral then, but interest has skyrocketed with Sunday's World Cup final between Argentina and Spain approaching. Monfort said he has been bombarded by queries for the photos by professional media outlets while also seeing his images reproduced countless times on social media and the internet without any credit or compensation.

 The 19-year-old Yamal will face a Messi who is 20 years his senior in Sunday's final. Monfort, 58, is considering traveling to see the final in New Jersey. He said his heart is split and he does not know if he wants Messi or Yamal to win.

hero.headline: TCT’s 2026 Summer Reading Picks: 12 Books to Add to Your List
hero.teaser: From brand-new memoirs and literary thrillers to romance, historical fiction and enduring American classics, these 12 books offer a summer reading option for nearly every mood.
hero.body:
Summer reading does not have to mean one particular kind of book. Some days call for a fast-moving crime story or romance that can keep you turning pages by the pool. Others are better suited to a searching memoir, an immersive family saga or a work of nonfiction that leaves you thinking long after you close it.

TCT's 2026 summer reading picks range from newly released books by Colson Whitehead, Tayari Jones, Annie Jacobsen, Patrick Radden Keefe and other major writers to modern favorites and classics worth discovering for the first time. The list includes literary fiction, memoir, romance, true crime, historical fiction and two enduring American novels.

Every synopsis below is intentionally spoiler-free. Use the Quick Picks section to browse the full list, then choose the book that best fits your current reading mood.

All That's Unseen: An Appalachian Memoir by Emilee Hackney

Memoir Pick

In this debut memoir, Emilee Hackney looks back on growing up in the coalfields of southwest Virginia, where family stories, Pentecostal faith and Appalachian identity shaped nearly every part of her world. As the boundaries around her life tighten, an unexpected path to Harvard begins a difficult reexamination of home, belief and her right to trust her own voice.

Memoir readers interested in Appalachia, faith and reclaiming one's voice

A personal story that treats Appalachia with both affection and clear-eyed honesty A strong choice for readers drawn to memoirs about faith, family and self-reinvention

Unsayable: A Life in Writing by Michael Cunningham

For Writers

Michael Cunningham blends memoir with a meditation on the writing life, moving through childhood, first love, early adulthood, marriage and the long process of becoming an author. Rather than offering a conventional how-to manual, he explores why writers keep trying to describe experiences that language can never capture completely.

Writers, devoted readers and anyone curious about how stories take shape

Combines intimate life writing with thoughtful reflections on literary craft Offers inspiration without pretending that creativity follows a simple formula

Cool Machine: A Novel (The Harlem Trilogy) by Colson Whitehead

Crime Fiction Pick

The final volume of Colson Whitehead's Harlem Trilogy follows furniture dealer and reluctant fence Ray Carney and his formidable partner Pepper through three episodes in 1980s New York. A last heist, the downtown art scene and an old family obligation pull them back toward the criminal world as the city around them becomes wealthier, glossier and no less dangerous.

Crime-fiction fans and readers of Whitehead's Harlem Trilogy

A propulsive crime story set against a sharply observed New York in transition The concluding chapter for readers who followed Harlem Shuffle and Crook Manifesto

Country People by Daniel Mason

Literary Escape

Miles Krzelewski is a loving husband and father who is twelve years late finishing a doctorate on Russian folktales. When his wife accepts a position in Vermont, he treats the move as a chance to restart his stalled life. Instead, he falls in with an eccentric cast of neighbors and becomes increasingly fascinated by a strange local legend that may be more than a story.

Readers who like witty literary fiction with folklore and small-town eccentricity

Balances family life, humor, folklore and a gently mysterious premise A summery change-of-scenery novel with an appealingly unusual cast

Kin by Tayari Jones

Book Club Pick

Vernice and Annie grow up as motherless best friends and neighbors in Honeysuckle, Louisiana, but adulthood sends them toward very different worlds. One leaves for Spelman College and a new circle of opportunity; the other follows a restless search for the mother who left her behind. Their stories eventually converge again in a novel about friendship, chosen family and the lasting pull of home.

Book clubs and readers of multigenerational Southern literary fiction

An emotionally rich story of lifelong friendship and diverging paths Built for discussion about family, ambition, belonging and the American South

Biological War: A Scenario by Annie Jacobsen

High-Stakes Nonfiction

Journalist Annie Jacobsen examines how a laboratory accident or deliberate biological attack could develop into a global emergency. Drawing on interviews with experts in government, medicine, science and the military, she traces a possible breakdown across hours, days and weeks, focusing on the systems meant to contain a fast-moving biological threat.

Readers of investigative journalism, public health and national-security nonfiction

Turns a complex national-security subject into an urgent chronological narrative A natural follow-up for readers of Nuclear War: A Scenario

London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe

True Crime Pick

After nineteen-year-old Zac Brettler dies in London, his grieving family begins asking questions that the official explanation does not settle. Their search reveals that Zac had constructed an elaborate second identity and become connected to figures in a dangerous criminal world. Patrick Radden Keefe follows the family through a story of grief, deception and the hidden networks beneath modern London.

Fans of narrative nonfiction, true crime and investigative mysteries

A deeply reported mystery driven by a family's determination to understand what happened Combines intimate human stakes with an investigation into wealth, identity and crime

Great Big Beautiful Life by Emily Henry

Romance Pick

Optimistic writer Alice Scott and Pulitzer-winning journalist Hayden Anderson arrive on a secluded island competing for the same assignment: the chance to write the biography of reclusive heiress Margaret Ives. Margaret gives each writer only pieces of her story and binds them with strict confidentiality, turning their professional rivalry into a literary mystery complicated by an inconvenient attraction.

Romance readers who like writer protagonists and a layered family mystery

Blends romance with a mystery about memory, storytelling and who controls a life story A beach-friendly choice for readers who enjoy sharp banter and slow-building chemistry

My Friends by Fredrik Backman

Friendship Story

Twenty-five years ago, four teenagers found refuge from difficult home lives during long summer days on an abandoned pier. Their friendship eventually inspired a remarkable painting that unexpectedly comes into the care of eighteen-year-old Louisa. Her effort to understand the artwork sends her on a journey toward the seaside town where the friends' story began.

Readers who want a moving, hopeful story about friendship and art

A warm, emotional novel about the ways friendship and art outlive a single moment Moves between youthful connection and a later journey of discovery

The Nightingale by Kristin Hannah

Historical Fiction

In German-occupied France during World War II, sisters Vianne and Isabelle face the same war with very different temperaments. Vianne tries to protect her home and child as danger closes in, while the younger and more defiant Isabelle is drawn toward active resistance. Their parallel stories explore survival, sacrifice and the often-overlooked choices women made during wartime.

Readers seeking sweeping, character-driven historical fiction

An accessible, emotionally intense entry point into World War II historical fiction Centers women's courage, moral choices and the complicated bonds between sisters

East of Eden by John Steinbeck

American Classic

Set in California's Salinas Valley, John Steinbeck's multigenerational novel follows the intertwined Trask and Hamilton families as patterns of rivalry, longing and betrayal echo across decades. Drawing on the biblical story of Cain and Abel, the novel asks whether people are trapped by inheritance and history or remain capable of choosing a different path.

Readers who want an ambitious multigenerational American classic

A sweeping family saga with memorable characters and enduring moral questions A substantial classic for readers ready to settle into a long summer novel

Their Eyes Were Watching God by Zora Neale Hurston

Florida Classic

Zora Neale Hurston's Florida-set classic follows Janie Crawford as she looks back on a life shaped by three marriages, changing ideas of love and a persistent desire to speak in her own voice. Written with lyricism, humor and vivid dialogue, Janie's journey moves through communities and relationships while tracing her growth toward independence and self-knowledge.

Readers of literary classics, Florida history and stories of self-discovery

An essential American novel with a strong Florida connection Combines a deeply personal search for freedom with Hurston's distinctive language and sense of place

A good summer reading list should offer more than one mood. Readers looking for a recent release can start with All That's Unseen, Cool Machine, Country People, Kin, Biological War or Unsayable. Those who want an emotional novel may gravitate toward My Friends, Great Big Beautiful Life or The Nightingale, while East of Eden and Their Eyes Were Watching God provide two very different ways to spend time with an American classic.

Book prices and availability can change, so use the links above to check the current format and price before ordering. Whichever title you choose, the best summer pick is the one that makes you look forward to finding another quiet hour to read.

cards.headline: Big Brothers Big Sisters returns Big Taste of Martin County fundraiser to Stuart
cards.teaser: Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties will hold the Big Taste of Martin County food and spirits event October 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart to support mentoring programs.
cards.body:
Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties is preparing for the return of Big Taste of Martin County, a food and spirits event scheduled for October 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart. The annual fundraiser brings together local restaurants, chefs and community partners to support mentoring programs for children across the Treasure Coast. Guests can sample food, wine and beer from area businesses while participating restaurants compete for Big Taste awards and local bragging rights.

 The event helps fund mentorship opportunities for children who are currently waiting to be matched with a mentor, known as a Big, according to Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties. The nonprofit said community members can support the mission by purchasing tickets, attending the event or volunteering to become a mentor. Spritz Stuart plans to feature several menu items during the event promotion, including a Tuscan salmon dish, a smash burger and a specialty cocktail called the Fig & Flame.

 Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties serves children and families throughout Palm Beach and Martin counties through one-on-one mentoring relationships designed to support academic achievement, confidence and personal growth. More information about the event and mentorship opportunities is available through Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Museum of Art to host recycled fishing line bracelet workshop Aug. 8
cards.teaser: The Vero Beach Museum of Art and Coastal Connections will team up for a free Second Saturday program starting at 10 a.m. Aug. 8.
cards.body:
The Vero Beach Museum of Art and Coastal Connections will host a free Second Saturday program beginning at 10 a.m. Aug. 8, with hands-on activities, gallery tours and lessons about protecting local marine life. Coastal Connections will lead a hands-on activity in the Laura and Bill Buck Atrium, where visitors can make friendship bracelets using recycled fishing line collected from local waterways.

 Participants also can learn about the Fishing Line Recycling Program. The museum has adopted the fishing line recycling tube at the Riverside Park boat ramp. From 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., families can take short, docent-led gallery tours through the Museum Studios family program.

 Visitors can then participate in Nature in Layers, an art activity for children connected to the museum's exhibitions. Guests also can tour the museum's summer exhibitions throughout the day. James Prosek: At Work is on view in the Holmes Gallery, while Jill Nathanson: Chromatic Phrases is displayed in the Schumann and Titelman galleries. Second Saturday includes free museum admission throughout the day.
