The Treasure Coast offers several family events this weekend, including a Christmas in July vendor market in Palm City and the weekly Rockn Riverwalk concert series in Stuart. The Christmas in July event takes place Saturday at 10 a.m. at 2001 SW Murphy Road in Palm City. The market will feature food trucks, an ornament decorating station and vendors.

 The Downtown Business Association of Stuart is hosting Rockn Riverwalk on Sunday at 1 p.m. on St. Lucie Avenue in Stuart. The free open-air concert series takes place every Sunday on the Riverwalk Stage, offering live music on the waterfront.

 Several additional events are scheduled in Palm Beach County this weekend. The Boynton Beach Night Market returns Saturday at 5 p.m. at Centennial Park and Amphitheater. The free event features vendors, food and live music connecting residents to the local business community.

 A back-to-school family festival will take place Sunday from noon to 5 p.m. at 7715 Forest Hill Boulevard in West Palm Beach, featuring games, food, music and a school supply giveaway. A school supply drive will also be held Saturday and Sunday at 10 a.m. at a Walmart at 101 N. Congress Avenue in Lake Park, with donations distributed at a Back to School Bash in August.

cards.headline: Boca Raton TLC Program Offers Summer Service Projects for South Florida Families
cards.teaser: B'nai Torah Congregation's TLC Program connects volunteers with hands-on service projects ranging from food support and shoe donations to pantry stocking and literacy efforts.
cards.body:
B'nai Torah Congregation's TLC Program is offering South Florida families a range of hands-on service projects this summer, from food support and shoe donations to pantry stocking, literacy efforts and care for seniors. Led by Summer Faerman, the program connects volunteers of all ages with mitzvah opportunities, or meaningful good deeds, as part of the congregation's broader community outreach efforts.

 The TLC Program stands for Tzedakah, Learning and Chesed, and has made service a central part of synagogue life since 2012. The program provides a way for individuals and families to put Jewish values into action while helping people in need across South Florida. It addresses multiple community concerns including hunger, homelessness, literacy, elder care, vulnerable populations and special needs. Organizers emphasize that the projects are open to everyone in the community, not only members of B'nai Torah Congregation, with the goal of making service practical, welcoming and easy to begin.

 Participants can volunteer in various ways throughout the summer. Projects include making sandwiches, serving meals, collecting and cleaning shoes, stocking Little Free Pantries, preparing backpacks for back-to-school efforts, creating Bags of Hope and helping seniors with technology. Organizers plan to demonstrate volunteer projects such as wrapping presents, making flower arrangements, preparing sandwiches, collecting shoes and assembling supplies for people in need. The variety of options allows families to choose activities that match their interests and schedules.

 As summer continues, the TLC Program offers families a way to stay connected, teach children about giving back and support neighbors throughout South Florida. B'nai Torah Congregation says the program is built around the idea that small acts of service can strengthen the larger community. More information about the TLC Program is available through B'nai Torah Congregation's website.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Food Bank serves 2,500 hot meals daily to children at 35 summer sites
cards.teaser: The Palm Beach County Food Bank in Lake Worth Beach is serving approximately 2,500 hot meals each day to nearly 1,250 children through Florida's Summer BreakSpot program while school is out.
cards.body:
The Palm Beach County Food Bank is serving approximately 2,500 hot meals each day to nearly 1,250 children through Florida's Summer BreakSpot program, according to Food Bank leaders. The nonprofit organization supports more than 35 Summer BreakSpot sites across Palm Beach County while school is out for the summer. During a live Shining A Light broadcast on WPTV, CEO Jamie Kendall and Culinary Director Chef Doug Barg gave viewers a behind-the-scenes look inside the Michelle Hagerty Community Kitchen, where meals are prepared and loaded onto trucks for early morning deliveries across the county.

 The organization prepared more than 36,000 hot meals in June alone. According to the Palm Beach County Food Bank, hunger doesn't take a summer break, highlighting the need for continued support during the summer months. The Summer BreakSpot program provides free meals to children and teens 18 and younger during the summer when school cafeterias are closed. Food Bank leaders said the meals are distributed through partner locations across Palm Beach County to help families facing food insecurity during the summer. Kendall said the Food Bank's partnership with Summer BreakSpot helps ensure children continue receiving nutritious meals while school is out.

 During the broadcast, viewers got a close look at the large-scale kitchen operation responsible for preparing meals daily. Chef Barg walked viewers through the food production process, showing how culinary teams prepare, package and organize meals before they are loaded onto delivery trucks. The loading dock operation featured drivers and volunteers preparing for morning deliveries to Summer BreakSpot sites throughout Palm Beach County. The Palm Beach County Food Bank said volunteers and community support are critical to maintaining the program during the busy summer season.

 The Palm Beach County Food Bank is located at 701 Boutwell Road, Suite A-1, in Lake Worth Beach. Food Bank leaders said the organization continues seeking volunteers, donations and community partnerships to support its mission of reducing childhood hunger in Palm Beach County. Families looking for Summer BreakSpot meal locations can find participating sites throughout the county during the summer months.

cards.headline: Downtown Delray Beach launches Wellness Pass with free fitness classes and spa deals for July and August
cards.teaser: The Delray Beach Downtown Development Authority launched the Downtown Delray Wellness Pass for July and August. The mobile-exclusive pass allows users to access complimentary classes, discounted wellness treatments and promotions from participating businesses.
cards.body:
Downtown Delray Beach is encouraging residents and visitors to prioritize health and self-care this summer through a new Wellness Pass featuring free fitness classes, yoga sessions, spa discounts and wellness-focused offers across the city's downtown district. The Delray Beach Downtown Development Authority launched the Downtown Delray Wellness Pass for July and August.

 According to the DDA, the mobile-exclusive pass allows users to access complimentary classes, discounted wellness treatments and promotions from participating businesses throughout Downtown Delray Beach. The pass does not require an app download. Miller Physical Therapy is also participating with wellness-related services and promotions. The program arrives as wellness tourism and fitness-focused experiences continue to grow in popularity across South Florida. Many consumers are seeking affordable ways to stay active, reduce stress and support local businesses during the summer months.

hero.headline: Florida judge considers challenge to Amendment 3 ballot language on property taxes
hero.teaser: A Leon County circuit judge heard arguments Wednesday over whether the ballot title and summary for Amendment 3, a November property-tax measure, fairly explains the proposal or am
hero.body:
A Leon County circuit judge heard arguments Wednesday over whether the ballot title and summary for Amendment 3, a November property-tax measure, fairly explains the proposal or amounts to political advocacy. The amendment would increase the non-school homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 for people who establish permanent Florida residency by Dec. 31, reduce the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead property from 10% to 5%, and require local governments to spend remaining property-tax revenue on public needs such as public safety, schools, infrastructure and natural resources.

Leon County Circuit Judge David Frank heard arguments in three consolidated lawsuits challenging the title and summary scheduled to appear on November ballots. The challengers include the nonprofit Save Our Voters From Misleading Ballot Language, several former mayors, former Republican state Sen. Jeff Brandes and former Democratic U.S. Rep. Al Lawson Jr. They argue the amendment's title, 'Save Our Homes From Excessive Property Taxes,' and phrases promising to benefit taxpayers, protect small businesses, preserve core services and ensure fairness are biased, inaccurate and designed to persuade voters. Plaintiffs' attorney Jamie Cole told the court the language crosses a line and called it the worst example of a biased ballot question he has seen. Frank did not immediately rule, instead ordering attorneys to submit proposed decisions by 5 p.m. Monday.

Attorneys representing the attorney general, secretary of state and Department of State urged Frank to uphold the language. State attorney Ben Gibson argued the title and summary must be read together and that Florida law requires them to explain only the amendment's chief purpose, not every possible consequence or implementation detail. The challengers must prove the title and summary are clearly and conclusively defective, not merely that different wording could have been better, Gibson said. The Legislature approved the proposal during a June special session, passing it 75-26 in the House and 30-9 in the Senate. Because it is a proposed constitutional amendment, it was not subject to the governor's signature or veto. It needs support from at least 60% of voters in November.

A July analysis by Florida's Revenue Estimating Conference projected the quantifiable portions of the amendment would reduce local property-tax collections by nearly $4.93 billion in the 2027-28 fiscal year. The modeled recurring impact is approximately $11.83 billion annually. Election officials told the court that county supervisors may begin printing ballots Aug. 27, adding urgency to the case and any appeal. If Frank finds all of the ballot statements defective and appeals are declined or exhausted, Florida law gives Attorney General James Uthmeier 10 days to submit corrected wording.

cards.headline: Florida executes former police officer convicted of killing 11-year-old girl in 1987
cards.teaser: James Aren Duckett, 68, was pronounced dead at 1:19 p.m. Tuesday at Florida State Prison, the first of two executions carried out by the state in a single day.
cards.body:
Duckett was convicted of raping and drowning 11-year-old Teresa McAbee while he was working as a police officer in central Florida in 1987. He declined to make a final statement and showed no response several minutes into the execution when the prison warden shook him and shouted his name. Duckett became the 11th Florida inmate executed this year.

 The girl's relatives spoke of decades of suffering after the execution. Dorthy Tula, the victim's mother, said she waited nearly 40 years to have him dead before breaking down. Tracy Mcfall-Buskirk, the girl's cousin, said the man took advantage of his badge. The execution was part of the first double execution in Florida in more than six decades and the first time any state has carried out two executions in one day since Arkansas in 2017.

 Florida has now conducted 12 executions to date in 2026, more than all other states combined. Gov. Ron DeSantis, who leaves office in January, oversaw a record 19 executions last year, more in a single year than any other Florida governor since the reinstatement of the death penalty in the U.S. in 1976.

cards.headline: Judge keeps Fishback on Florida Republican primary ballot, rejects Collins residency challenge
cards.teaser: Lt. Gov. Jay Collins failed to remove gubernatorial candidate James Fishback from Florida's Republican primary ballot after a judge ruled Collins did not present enough evidence to prove Fishback abandoned his Florida residency.
cards.body:
Circuit Judge David Frank ruled Monday that Collins failed to present enough evidence to overcome Florida's legal presumptions favoring continued residency and access to the ballot. Collins argued that Fishback failed to satisfy the Florida Constitution's requirement that a governor reside in the state for the seven years preceding the general election. Collins attorneys pointed to records showing Fishback voted in Washington during the 2020 presidential election, filed D.C. resident income-tax returns and signed mortgage documents identifying a condominium there as his principal residence.

 Fishback testified that he never intended to abandon Florida as his permanent home. He described the Washington property as a second residence or investment and said he signed the mortgage documents without closely reviewing them. Frank acknowledged that Fishback's filings could potentially create legal or regulatory consequences in Washington.

 But he found that they did not establish that Fishback intended to surrender his Florida domicile. The judge also cited Fishback's Florida upbringing, family connections, drivers license, vehicle registration, voting history and business ties to the state.

 The order leaves Fishback on the Aug. 18 Republican primary ballot. Fishback turned his courtroom victory into a campaign counterattack Tuesday, demanding that Collins resign and accusing the lieutenant governor of abusing his office and the public trust by pursuing the residency challenge. Collins rejected the resignation demand and said the ruling would not change his campaign.

 A Cygnal survey conducted July 12 and 13 placed U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds, the Trump-endorsed Republican frontrunner, at 43%, Fishback at 12%, Collins at 11% and former Florida House Speaker Paul Renner at 2%.

cards.headline: Over 150 assisted living residents remain displaced after Bradenton roof collapse
cards.teaser: More than 150 Florida residents remain scattered across assisted living facilities throughout the Tampa Bay area days after a partial roof collapse forced an emergency evacuation at Aviata at Bradenton Villas early Sunday morning.
cards.body:
Family members and advocates say loved ones have been placed in facilities as far south as Englewood and as far north as New Port Richey, with medical records, wheelchairs and personal belongings still trapped inside the damaged building. George Mendez, who holds power of attorney for 93-year-old Alfred Perani, came to the facility Monday after repeated phone calls to Aviata Health Group went unanswered.

 Perani, who has been a resident at Aviata at Bradenton Villas for three years, was evacuated to a facility in Palm Harbor. Mendez found an available bed at another facility in Bradenton to bring his friend closer to home but says he cannot complete the transfer without Perani's medical records.

 In a joint statement released Monday, the City of Bradenton and Manatee County provided new details about why the Fire Marshal ordered the emergency evacuation. Officials say the partial roof collapse compromised multiple building systems essential to safe operation, including fire protection, electrical and air conditioning systems. Damage to critical support areas necessary for resident care, combined with the inability to safely complete a full structural assessment during the emergency, made it unsafe for residents to remain.

 The emergency response involved the City of Bradenton Fire Department, Manatee County Public Safety and Emergency Medical Services, and multiple regional partners. All 157 residents were evacuated by approximately 4 a.m. Sunday.

 The City of Bradenton is in charge of the building assessment. A city spokesperson confirmed that city officials and the Fire Marshal were on-site at Aviata Monday, along with flooding and restoration specialists. According to the joint statement, the property owner's structural engineer is responsible for evaluating the building, and any determination regarding the cause of the collapse will be based on that evaluation. The Agency for Health Care Administration is conducting site visits at the facilities where residents were relocated as part of its state regulatory oversight.

cards.headline: Florida executes two inmates in single day for first time in more than 60 years
cards.teaser: Florida on Tuesday carried out two executions in a single day, the first state to do so in nearly a decade. Dominick Anthony Occhicone, 80, was pronounced dead at 6:13 p.m. at Flor
cards.body:
Florida on Tuesday carried out two executions in a single day, the first state to do so in nearly a decade. Dominick Anthony Occhicone, 80, was pronounced dead at 6:13 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke, nearly five hours after James Aren Duckett, 68, received a lethal injection in the same death chamber. Occhicone became the second-oldest inmate known to receive a lethal injection in modern U.S. history and the oldest known prisoner executed in Florida since the state began modern record-keeping a century ago.

 Duckett, a former police officer, was convicted of raping and drowning 11-year-old Teresa McAbee in central Florida in 1987. Occhicone was convicted of fatally shooting his ex-girlfriends parents in June 1986.

 Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has the authority under Florida law to set execution dates, decided earlier this month to carry out both executions on the same day. The lethal injections several hours apart were the first nearly back-to-back executions since Arkansas put two men to death three hours apart in 2017.

 Florida Department of Corrections records show multiple executions on a single day were more common in the past, the last being in 1964. The U.S. Supreme Court denied last appeals from both men Tuesday.

 Florida has become the nation's busiest death chamber as DeSantis approaches the end of his final term in office. Since 2025 began, Florida has carried out nearly half the state executions across the country. Duckett became the 11th Florida inmate executed this year, and Florida leads the nation with 12 executions to date in 2026, more than all other states combined.

 DeSantis oversaw a record 19 executions last year, more in a single year than any other Florida governor since the U.S. reinstatement of the death penalty in 1976. Nationwide, a total of 19 executions including Tuesday's have been carried out this year.

 Another execution in Florida is set for August. All Florida executions are by injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections. DeSantis has rarely commented on the pace of executions, previously noting some on death row had committed crimes as far back as the 1980s. The governor said last year he felt he owed it to victims' families to make sure executions ran smoothly.

cards.headline: Florida ticket wins $800 million Mega Millions jackpot sold at Bradenton Wawa
cards.teaser: A winning Mega Millions ticket matching all six numbers in Tuesday's drawing was sold at a Wawa in Bradenton, ending a streak of 38 drawings without a winner.
cards.body:
A winning Mega Millions ticket was sold in Florida, as it was the only ticket to match all six numbers in Tuesday's drawing. The jackpot is worth $800 million, or an estimated $344 million cash option. The winning numbers were the white balls 34, 48, 49, 59 and 70, plus the gold Mega Ball 12. The ticket was sold at a Wawa located at 14510 State Road 70 East in Bradenton.

 Tuesday's drawing ended a streak of 38 drawings without a winner. It is the largest jackpot win of 2026 so far. Tuesday also marked the third jackpot win for Mega Millions in 2026.

 The last time a winning ticket was sold was March 17 in Ohio. The odds of matching all six numbers are about 1 in 290 million. Mega Millions is played in 45 states, plus the District of Columbia and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

cards.headline: Florida voters to decide November referendum on raising homestead exemption for property tax reform
cards.teaser: A November referendum will ask Florida voters to raise the homestead exemption as part of proposed property tax reform, generating strong debate over potential savings for homeowners and reduced revenue for cities and counties.
cards.body:
Florida voters will decide in November on a referendum to raise the homestead exemption as part of a proposed property tax reform. Sean Kelly of Lantana said he supports the referendum even though he does not own a home, believing it will bring accountability back where it should be. Kelly said the potential savings are meaningful, especially given other rising costs, and that saving $2,000 or $3,000 could help offset increases in home insurance.

 Cities and counties say the reduced revenue will strain budgets and leave them looking for other revenue streams through fees and other taxes. Former state Sen. Jeff Brandes said local governments will push back, predicting a large organization campaign to educate voters on the issue of ad valorem taxation and reduction of services or increased millage.

 Kelly said he does not believe local governments would suffer, arguing they need to look at how they spend their budget. He said he thinks municipalities will look to limit spending and put taxpayers more in control.

hero.headline: More Than 70 Animals Found in Stuart Home During Large-Scale Hoarding Response
hero.teaser: 77-year-old Gail Giustino was arrested on two misdemeanor animal cruelty-related charges following the search of a Stuart home where Martin County authorities found more than 70 an
hero.body:
More than a dozen animals from a Martin County hoarding case have found forever homes and the total number of rescued dogs and cats has climbed to 108. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says animals continue to come in from the same case. Sarah Fisher of the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast said every single day more animals are coming forth from the same case.

Fisher said the shelter needs community support to keep up with the growing number of animals in its care. Donations have been pouring in as staff perform spay and neuter surgeries, microchip animals, and clear them medically for adoption every day. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast recommends checking their website for the most up-to-date adoption listings. Those interested in adopting can call or visit the shelter for a meet and greet.

cards.headline: Martin County School District cuts 3 bus routes, saving $255,000
cards.teaser: The Martin County School District has approved a consolidation of bus routes that officials say will save $255,000 without affecting students or eliminating any driver positions.
cards.body:
The Martin County School District has approved a consolidation of bus routes that officials say will save $255,000 without affecting students or eliminating any driver positions. The school board voted Tuesday unanimously to reduce the number of bus routes by 3, bringing the total from 58 to 55 ahead of the upcoming school year. District officials say all bus stops will remain the same and students will not be impacted by the change. Superintendent Michael Maine said the district now has 55 routes and roughly 56 drivers, so all routes are covered.

The $255,000 in savings reflects a reduced transportation budget and will not be redirected to a specific expense, according to the school district. Transportation Director Ruth Spires confirmed that no drivers were let go as part of the consolidation. She said the routes that were consolidated were already being covered by existing drivers due to a shortage last year. Drivers will be paid for any additional hours they work as a result of the consolidation, Spires explained.

Michael Skinner, the President of the local AFSCME labor union chapter, voiced concerns during public comment on behalf of the bus drivers, saying their feedback indicated buses are always full and cutting routes is not a good idea. Spires pushed back on that concern, noting that the buses hold a maximum of 77 passengers and are not operating at capacity. The district said it is confident it will maintain the same level of service with fewer buses on the road.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue faces $16.5M loss, 116 job cuts if property tax reform passes
cards.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue could lose $16.5 million if voters approve property tax reform in November, according to public records. County commissioners are set to discuss what thos
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli warned Tuesday that a proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could reduce Fire Rescue funding by $9.5 million in the first year and $16.5 million annually by the second year, potentially forcing the closure of three fire stations and the layoff of 116 firefighters. The measure, which will go before Florida voters in November, could lower property tax bills for homeowners but also reduce revenue used to pay for public services. During Tuesday's Martin County Commission meeting, Cianciulli presented a planning exercise outlining how his department could respond to the projected revenue loss.

Under the scenario, Fire Rescue could close Station 18 on Britt Road, Station 33 in Hobe Sound, and Station 23 on Kanner Highway. The $16.5 million annual loss by the second year represents a 22 percent reduction from the department's current budget. The chief said the department could be forced to lay off as many as 116 firefighters by the second year, equivalent to one of the department's three shifts.

Cianciulli warned the funding loss could force Martin County to eliminate specialized teams responsible for hazardous materials incidents, technical rescues and dive operations. The department could then have to request assistance from neighboring agencies in Palm Beach or St. Lucie counties, potentially increasing response times. In an interview after the meeting, Cianciulli pointed to the deadly Camp Mystic flooding in Texas as an example of the delays that can occur when a community must rely on outside resources. He said Martin County already has difficulty recruiting trained firefighter-paramedics because departments farther south offer better compensation.

County leaders have previously said the department has few options to absorb the projected revenue loss because about 93 percent of the Fire Rescue budget is dedicated to personnel. Martin County Commissioner James Blake Capps said higher insurance premiums could result from station closures, as residents living more than five miles from a fire station pay higher homeowner's insurance. Cianciulli advised residents to learn as much as possible about the proposal and its potential effects before casting their ballots in November.

cards.headline: Big Brothers Big Sisters returns Big Taste of Martin County fundraiser to Stuart
cards.teaser: Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties will hold the Big Taste of Martin County food and spirits event October 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart to support mentoring programs.
cards.body:
Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties is preparing for the return of Big Taste of Martin County, a food and spirits event scheduled for October 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart. The annual fundraiser brings together local restaurants, chefs and community partners to support mentoring programs for children across the Treasure Coast. Guests can sample food, wine and beer from area businesses while participating restaurants compete for Big Taste awards and local bragging rights.

 The event helps fund mentorship opportunities for children who are currently waiting to be matched with a mentor, known as a Big, according to Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties. The nonprofit said community members can support the mission by purchasing tickets, attending the event or volunteering to become a mentor. Spritz Stuart plans to feature several menu items during the event promotion, including a Tuscan salmon dish, a smash burger and a specialty cocktail called the Fig & Flame.

 Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties serves children and families throughout Palm Beach and Martin counties through one-on-one mentoring relationships designed to support academic achievement, confidence and personal growth. More information about the event and mentorship opportunities is available through Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties.

 The Downtown Business Association of Stuart is hosting Rockn Riverwalk on Sunday at 1 p.m. on St. Lucie Avenue in Stuart. The free open-air concert series takes place every Sunday on the Riverwalk Stage, offering live music on the waterfront.

 Several additional events are scheduled in Palm Beach County this weekend. The Boynton Beach Night Market returns Saturday at 5 p.m. at Centennial Park and Amphitheater. The free event features vendors, food and live music connecting residents to the local business community.

cards.headline: Martin County moves to rewrite shark fishing rules after complaints about drones, chum
cards.teaser: Martin County commissioners are rewriting beach fishing rules after complaints that shark fishermen are using drones and remote-controlled boats to drop chum offshore and lure sharks closer to swimming areas.
cards.body:
Martin County commissioners are rewriting the rules on fishing from public beaches after complaints that shark fishermen are using drones and remote-controlled boats to drop chum offshore and lure sharks closer to swimming areas. County attorneys told commissioners Tuesday that Florida law allows fishing from public beaches and takes precedence over conflicting county ordinances. Commissioners now plan to repeal or rewrite portions of the county's existing law and replace them with restrictions based on public safety.

 Shark fishing has grown increasingly popular in Martin County, according to residents who addressed commissioners. Some said they are concerned fishermen are putting swimmers at risk by attracting sharks close to shore. Chumming directly from the beach is already prohibited under Florida law, but commissioners heard complaints that some fishermen are using drones or remote-controlled boats to carry bait offshore before dropping it into the water, potentially allowing them to skirt the state restriction.

 County attorneys recommended drafting a new ordinance that complies with state fishing laws while relying on the county's authority to protect public safety and welfare. Under the proposal, fishing could be prohibited from county beaches during lifeguard hours, when swimmers are most likely to be in the water. The revised ordinance would also prohibit fishing from boat docks while boats are being launched or returning to shore. Commissioners directed county staff to draft the new ordinance and bring it back for a future vote.

cards.headline: Martin County School District consolidates bus routes to save $255,000
cards.teaser: The Martin County School District approved changes to its bus routes for the upcoming school year, aiming to improve efficiency and reduce costs.
cards.body:
The Martin County School District approved changes to its bus routes for the upcoming school year, aiming to improve efficiency and reduce costs. The new routes, which will begin on August 10, will consolidate existing routes while keeping bus stops and buses unchanged from last year. The district said the changes will save $255,000.

 The changes address a decline in ridership and will save the district the cost of operating three bus routes, according to Ruth, the district's director of transportation. The district also cited a shortage of bus drivers as part of the reason for the decision. No jobs were lost as a result of the changes.

 Parents can track their child's bus route in real time using the MyReaxium app. The route changes also include activity buses for after-school programs.

hero.headline: Neighbor on Silverstream Circle says community worried about child before Fort Pierce infant death
hero.teaser: A neighbor who lived on Silverstream Circle in Fort Pierce for more than a decade said the community worried about how the 3-month-old was being treated but never thought it was that bad.
hero.body:
Tee McMillan, who lived near the Maxwell home on Silverstream Circle in Fort Pierce for more than a decade, said the death of the infant boy is heartbreaking and haunts her. McMillan said when that baby boy died it was just the worst of the worst. She said everyone in the neighborhood worried about how the child was treated but never knew it was that bad.

McMillan said the community never thought that a baby boy would die. She said all anyone wants is justice for the baby. Deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center after the child was brought to the emergency room by the child's grandparents and medical personnel advised responding deputies that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce residents fight plan to replace Museum Pointe Park with mega-yacht marina
cards.teaser: A proposal to transform Museum Pointe, a public waterfront park in Fort Pierce along the Indian River Lagoon, into a mega-yacht marina has drawn nearly 800 petition signatures from
cards.body:
A proposal to transform Museum Pointe, a public waterfront park in Fort Pierce along the Indian River Lagoon, into a mega-yacht marina has drawn nearly 800 petition signatures from opponents. The Port of Fort Pierce's updated 2026 Master Plan calls for redeveloping the park, which currently features a history center, public waterfront access, fishing piers, and green space, into a facility with floating docks, a multi-story marina, an event center, a waterfront restaurant, and a clubhouse.

 Terry Howard, a volunteer at the History Center at Museum Pointe Park, said development threatens one of the city's most treasured public spaces. The museum has preserved artifacts from Florida's Native American tribes, Spanish shipwrecks, and more for over 50 years. The master plan's renderings place the proposed marina clubhouse exactly where the museum stands today.

 Howard said the concern extends beyond the museum's fate to the loss of public waterfront access. St. Lucie County spokesperson Erick Gill said the museum's future is not in jeopardy if the project moves forward, and that staff has been discussing better locations for the history center for years because it sits on a barrier island in a flood zone.

 Gill said the museum and its collection would be preserved and relocated if the project proceeds. He added that the master plan is designed to expand economic development, create jobs, and generate county revenue. Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the city will have the final say on whether the project moves forward, and that commissioners will have to weigh economic benefits against preserving waterfront access. Broderick said the city must be careful not to eliminate public access to the waterway.

 St. Lucie County leaders are scheduled to discuss the proposal and its current status at a 9 a.m. meeting at the St. Lucie County Commission Chambers. Howard said the stakes go beyond the present. The museum has been at Museum Pointe since the 1970s, and once the area is developed, the public waterfront space will never be replaced.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County deputy fired after social media post mocked sheriff's performance standards
cards.teaser: A St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy was fired after an Internal Affairs investigation found she created a Facebook post mocking Sheriff Richard Del Toro's Standards of Performance.
cards.body:
A St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy was fired after an Internal Affairs investigation found she created a Facebook post mocking Sheriff Richard Del Toro's Standards of Performance. Deputy Tina Speicker was terminated on June 12, 2026, following an investigation that began when Del Toro was made aware of the post on Oct. 10, 2025.

 According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Internal Affairs report, Speicker posted an image titled Standards of Power that closely resembled Del Toro's official Standards of Performance, which outlined eight performance expectations introduced after he was sworn into office. Speicker's version replaced the original language with phrases depicting domination, manipulation and exploitation. The parody included statements such as Top-down domination, Keep everyone beneath you guessing who's next to take the blame, Display a ruthless work ethic with a focus on self-preservation, and Remain obsessive and paranoid.

 Investigators identified several similarities between the two graphics, including that both contained eight principles, used similar wording and sentence structure, began each bullet point with the same first word, and featured a similar two-tone outline. During interviews, Speicker acknowledged posting the graphic but claimed it was intended as commentary on Congress and the federal government shutdown, not the Sheriff's Office. Investigators rejected that explanation, concluding the graphic was intended to parody the Sheriff's official standards.

 The Internal Affairs report found Speicker gave inconsistent statements during multiple interviews. Investigators sustained allegations of criticism of orders or policies, conduct unbecoming, violating the code of ethics for public officers and employees, and false testimony. The investigation concluded Speicker violated Sheriff's Office policies on all four counts, leading to her termination.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie men flee police at 80 mph, one found hiding on roof of occupied home
cards.teaser: Two men led Port St. Lucie police on a high-speed chase before abandoning their car and fleeing on foot Monday, with one suspect found hiding on the roof of an occupied home.
cards.body:
A suspected drunk driver fled Port St. Lucie police at nearly 80 mph in a 45 mph zone before he and his passenger abandoned their car and ran. According to the Port St. Lucie Police Department, officers attempted to stop a white Acura after observing multiple traffic violations and signs of impaired driving on Southwest Becker Road. Instead of pulling over, the driver accelerated and weaved in and out of traffic, ignoring traffic signs and signals.

 The driver and passenger abandoned the vehicle in a residential driveway near Southwest Idol Avenue before fleeing on foot. A nearby resident called 911 after seeing the two men run from the scene. Police deployed a K-9 and a drone while officers established a perimeter. Both suspects were located, including one who was found hiding on the roof of an occupied home.

 The suspects were identified as Joseph Gary Harris, 42, and Bryan Shawn Baker, 46. Harris was charged with fleeing and eluding law enforcement, burglary of an occupied dwelling, resisting an officer without violence, and loitering or prowling. Baker was charged with resisting an officer without violence and loitering or prowling.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie bans gas station on Tradition commercial site after months of resident concerns
cards.teaser: The Port St. Lucie City Council has permanently banned construction of a gas station on a 9.4-acre commercial parcel at the southwest corner of Crosstown Parkway and Fairgreen Driv
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council has permanently banned construction of a gas station on a 9.4-acre commercial parcel at the southwest corner of Crosstown Parkway and Fairgreen Drive in Tradition. The council unanimously approved the restriction on July 13 as part of the 16th amendment to the Tradition Master Planned Unit Development, ending nearly three months of debate over the future of land originally planned as Phase 3 of the Heritage Oaks at Tradition residential development.

 Winding River Crosstown LLC requested permission in May to convert the parcel from residential to commercial use. While council members supported commercial development, several raised concerns that a convenience store with gas pumps would worsen traffic along Crosstown Parkway west of Interstate 95. Vice Mayor Jolien Caraballo and other council members asked staff to determine whether gas stations could be eliminated as a permitted use, leading the council to table the request on May 26. Heritage Oaks residents urged the council in June to reject the land-use change, citing traffic, noise and neighborhood impacts.

 The council voted 4-0 on June 22 to approve the commercial designation after the developer agreed to permanently give up the right to build a gas station. The July 13 ordinance codified that restriction into the Tradition MPUD documents, ensuring the prohibition remains with the property regardless of future ownership. City planner Bridget Kean said service stations remain permitted elsewhere in the Tradition mixed-use area but are now prohibited on Parcel 11A. The updated plan also requires the developer to install a fence along the southern property line before mass grading and to complete an architectural wall and landscape buffering along the southeastern and southern boundaries before the first building permit is issued.

 Councilman Anthony Bonna defended the public process and the decision, saying Port St. Lucie has long lacked commercial development, placing a burden on homeowners. Councilman David Pickett said the city has consistently heard residents oppose additional housing and called the shift to commercial the best outcome for the corner. Councilwoman Stephanie Morgan, who initially questioned whether prohibiting a specific business type amounted to government interference, ultimately voted with the council. Mayor Shannon Martin confirmed the restriction would remain with the property in perpetuity before the final unanimous vote.

cards.headline: 2 men force victim to withdraw cash at Wells Fargo ATM in Fort Pierce armed robbery
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police are searching for two men in their early 20s who forced a victim to withdraw cash at gunpoint from a Wells Fargo ATM on Sunday night.
cards.body:
A man using a Wells Fargo ATM in Fort Pierce became the victim of an armed robbery on Sunday at about 8:38 p.m. when two men forced him to pull out cash before fleeing on foot. The Fort Pierce Police Department said one of the men displayed a gun concealed in his waistband before forcing the victim to withdraw an unknown amount of cash. Officers responded to the scene, established a perimeter, and used a K-9 and drone to search for the suspects, but the suspects were not located.

 Police described the suspects as two men in their early 20s, about 5 feet 10 inches tall and weighing about 170 pounds. The armed suspect was last seen wearing jeans and a gray hooded sweatshirt. The Fort Pierce Police Department is asking anyone with information to contact the department.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce police seek help identifying suspects in Recreation Center vandalism and vehicle burglaries
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police are asking for the public's help identifying people shown in surveillance images connected to two separate investigations involving vandalism at the Fort Pierce Recreation Center and vehicle burglaries in the Lawnwood Circle area.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police are asking for the public's help identifying people shown in surveillance images connected to two separate investigations involving vandalism and vehicle burglaries. Police said the vandalism occurred at about 4 p.m. July 24 at the Fort Pierce Recreation Center, located at 903 S.

 An unidentified woman was captured on camera damaging city property. Police said multiple air-conditioning units, a trailer and a storage shed were damaged.

 The second investigation involves a series of vehicle burglaries reported during the overnight hours of July 27 in the Lawnwood Circle area. Police said the burglaries occurred in the 1300 block of Nebraska Avenue and the 1300 block of Peppertree Trail, primarily between 2 a.m. and 4 a.m. Investigators said several vehicles were burglarized.

 Some had been left unlocked, while others had windows smashed to gain entry. Surveillance footage showed several people in the area wearing hoodies, shorts and backpacks.

 The department stressed that the vandalism and vehicle burglary cases are separate investigations. Anyone who recognizes the people pictured or has information about either case is asked to contact Fort Pierce police at 772-467-6800 or 772-462-6800. Anonymous tips can be submitted to Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at tcwatch.org. Police also reminded residents to lock their vehicles, remove valuables from plain view and report suspicious activity immediately.

hero.headline: Vero Beach Museum of Art to host recycled fishing line bracelet workshop Aug. 8
hero.teaser: The Vero Beach Museum of Art and Coastal Connections will team up for a free Second Saturday program starting at 10 a.m. Aug. 8.
hero.body:
The Vero Beach Museum of Art and Coastal Connections will host a free Second Saturday program beginning at 10 a.m. Aug. 8, with hands-on activities, gallery tours and lessons about protecting local marine life. Coastal Connections will lead a hands-on activity in the Laura and Bill Buck Atrium, where visitors can make friendship bracelets using recycled fishing line collected from local waterways.

 Participants also can learn about the Fishing Line Recycling Program. The museum has adopted the fishing line recycling tube at the Riverside Park boat ramp. From 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., families can take short, docent-led gallery tours through the Museum Studios family program.

 Visitors can then participate in Nature in Layers, an art activity for children connected to the museum's exhibitions. Guests also can tour the museum's summer exhibitions throughout the day. James Prosek: At Work is on view in the Holmes Gallery, while Jill Nathanson: Chromatic Phrases is displayed in the Schumann and Titelman galleries. Second Saturday includes free museum admission throughout the day.

cards.headline: Indian River County firefighter and paramedic died by suicide in Sebastian, police report reveals
cards.teaser: Indian River County Fire Rescue firefighter and paramedic Geoffrey S. Lang, 35, died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound at his Sebastian home on Saturday, July 25, according to a
cards.body:
Indian River County Fire Rescue firefighter and paramedic Geoffrey S. Lang, 35, died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound at his Sebastian home on Saturday, July 25, according to a Sebastian Police Department report released Wednesday. Officers responded to Lang's residence at 4:18 p.m. after his wife called 911 to report that her husband had shot himself in front of her.

 Sebastian police officers arrived to find Lang's wife and a neighbor outside the residence. Officers entered the home with a K-9 dog and discovered Lang's body in a bedroom with an apparent gunshot wound to the head. An Indian River County Fire Rescue individual pronounced Lang dead at the scene. His body was transported to the medical examiner's office by Lowther Funeral Home.

 A neighbor told police they heard a woman yelling and screaming, followed by a single gunshot between 3 p.m. and 4 p.m. The neighbor initially thought the sound was fireworks but recognized it as a gunshot. After officers arrived, one neighbor reported speaking with a female neighbor who appeared hostile.

 A funeral service for Lang will be held Tuesday, August 3, at Community Church located at 1901 23rd Street. Anyone needing help can contact the Suicide Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988, or reach the 211 Helpline of Palm Beach and Treasure Coast by dialing 211 or texting their ZIP code to 898211.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County investigators say 3-month-old's death may bring further charges
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office investigators are examining the death of a 3-month-old baby in Fort Pierce that occurred in August of last year and say further charges could be pending against the caregivers.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office investigators identified the three caregivers as the baby's mother, Nicole Maxwell, the baby's grandfather, Robert Maxwell, and his girlfriend, Vikki Koon. Detective Corporal Jennifer Diaz said none of the caregivers could explain how the baby died. Findings from the medical examiner determined the cause of death was a lack of food and a lack of fluid intake, indicating the baby potentially was not properly being fed and due to the child's age, was unable to care for themselves.

 The baby and Nicole Maxwell's 9-year-old son, who has autism, lived in the mobile home with their grandfather and his girlfriend. Nicole Maxwell lived with her boyfriend in Vero Beach but would visit occasionally. Court records revealed Facebook messages between Nicole Maxwell and her father, Robert Maxwell, raising concerns about the infant's health.

 One message on Aug. 12 mentioned that the infant was out of food. Another message on Aug. 19 showed Nicole asking if the infant was okay. On Aug. 20, Robert Maxwell stated the infant had died.

 Diaz said she interviewed the mother and there were a lack of emotion and a lack of empathy towards the death of the child. All three caregivers remain in custody as the investigation continues. Authorities noted that the family has a history of involvement with the Department of Children and Families, and Maxwell's other children are currently in foster care.

cards.headline: Cyclist rides through Vero Beach on 2,600-mile journey from Key West to Maine
cards.teaser: A Boston cyclist rode through Vero Beach this week on a 2,600-mile bike ride from Key West to Maine to honor a friend lost to colorectal cancer.
cards.body:
Jay Weedall traveled to South Florida to begin the journey, with a goal of raising $50,000 for the Young Onset Colorectal Cancer Research Center. Weedall began his journey in Key West, pedaling 155 miles to Miami on day one. He set off on his second leg, a 163-mile ride to Vero Beach, after filling his hydration pack with ice to stay cool.

 Weedall is riding roughly 150 miles a day up the coast through nearly every state all the way to the Pan Mass Challenge. He will do the Pan Mass Challenge across Massachusetts on August 2 and continue to the Canadian border in Maine. By avoiding highways, Weedall says the route offers something unexpected, allowing him to experience little coastal towns along the inlets. Fans can follow Weedall's journey on the cycling app Strava.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Police Department honors service of Indian River County firefighter
cards.teaser: The Vero Beach Police Department said it stands with Indian River County Fire Rescue following the death of Firefighter Geoffrey Lang.
cards.body:
The Vero Beach Police Department said it stands alongside Indian River County Fire Rescue in mourning the loss of Firefighter Geoffrey Lang, who passed away while off duty. The department said its thoughts are with his family, loved ones and colleagues during this incredibly difficult time and that it honors his service and the impact he made on the community.

 Indian River County Fire Rescue announced Lang's death Saturday night and thanked neighboring agencies that quickly shared messages of support following the announcement. The Sebastian Police Department said it stands alongside its brothers and sisters of Indian River County Fire Rescue as they mourn the heartbreaking loss and that Lang's dedication, courage and commitment to serving others will never be forgotten.

cards.headline: Treasure Coast single-family home prices rise after two-year decline
cards.teaser: Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after drops from 2023 to 2025. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St.
cards.body:
Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after drops from 2023 to 2025. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000. Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000.

 Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that the prices are going to come back down. Inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers.

 Cara Collins, who bought her Martin County home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell. Collins said current prices are higher than she would hope for, and that the market has changed what would be possible for her family today. She said she would not be able to be a stay-at-home mom and be able to afford a home for her kids if buying now.

 Condos and townhomes show different trends. Prices have dropped in Martin and St. Lucie counties and only increased by less than a percent in Indian River County. Decowski said buyers need to come in pre-approved before they go looking at homes, and sellers need to price their homes realistically and present a well-maintained product.
